catalog_quote: Our knowledge of Oriomo prosody is vanishingly small: there is word-initial stress in Bine (Döhler, in press: 6), but for Wipi and Gizrra prosody is entirely undescribed. More detailed description may yet reveal complex prosody in these languages as well. [Josefsson 2025: 47] ... In Western Bine, at least, vowel length is marginally phonemic: a subset of vowels (a, i, u) contrast long and short pairs in word-initial (i.e., stressed) open syllables, e.g. kame '1SG.POSS' vs. kaame 'bush wallaby' (Döhler, in press: 6). [Josefsson 2025: 25] ... Length is contrastive for all vowels in the initial syllable of words and also in the initial syllable of each stem in compound words. [Fleischmann & Turpeinen 1977: 102] ... The suprasegmental system shows a complex stress system with rhythm principles, and apparently a two-tone system of very low functional load. [Wurm 1971: 146]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the first syllable of the word (reported second-hand from Döhler's in-press sketch, p. 6). Corroborated by the phonetic transcription of the text in Fleischmann & Turpeinen 1977: 138-140 (saved excerpt), where every word carries the primary-stress mark on its initial syllable, and by their statement (p. 102) that vowel length is contrastive 'in the initial syllable of words and also in the initial syllable of each stem in compound words'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated in any opened source. In the 1977 text transcription (pp. 138-140) a secondary mark (") appears on a later syllable of words of four or more syllables (e.g. 'ya:n:a"dzuge, 'mat(h)i"k(h)aeli, 'p(h)e:s:e"nene, 't(h)at(h)ja"rige), which looks like penultimate secondary stress, but this is my reading of the transcription, not a statement.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Wurm 1971: 146 (first-hand, family survey, saved) says Bine has 'a complex stress system with rhythm principles, and apparently a two-tone system of very low functional load' without giving a position; Josefsson 2025 does not treat Bine as tonal (only Meryam in the family). Bine function words are often shortened in rapid speech (Josefsson 2025: 51 fn. 1, after Döhler).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (word-initial stress; the vowel-length contrast is anchored to the word-initial stressed syllable and to the initial syllable of each stem in compounds per Fleischmann & Turpeinen 1977: 102). Citation forms and phrasal prominence not discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Josefsson 2025 and Döhler (in press) describe Western Bine (the Kunini/Masingle/Drageli varieties; Döhler groups eight Bine varieties into Western and Eastern); Fleischmann & Turpeinen 1977 describe Eastern Bine (SIL work 1970s). Both are dialects of bine1240 (no separate glottocodes in Glottolog 5.1). Wurm 1971 refers to Bine generally (Kunini dialect data).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is on the first syllable of the word. The heading promises tone, stress and length but the only sentence is the stress rule; vowel length is shown as phonemic in the inventory (aa, ee, ii, oo, uu, ää) and the syllable-pattern list. Nothing on tone.
new_statements.identity_note: The SIL materials (Fleischmann & Turpeinen 1977, Fleischmann 1970s/1981, Saari 1992) describe the Kunini dialect (eastern Bine, near Daru; 1977 data from four months in Kunini 1973-74; the OPD header mislabels the language code as [ORM]). Döhler's ELAR deposit and dictionary describe Irukupi/Drageli (western Bine; Döhler's own dialect paragraph has a typo calling both groups 'eastern'). All are bine1240 / ISO bon.

new_statements.quote: The phonological word consists of one or more rhythm units with one primary stress. Stress is predictable by the following rules: Primary stress (') occurs on the first syllable. In compound words it occurs on the first syllable of each stem, thereby forming two phonological words. [...] In verbs of more than three syllables secondary stress (") falls on the penultimate syllable. Tertiary stress ("') falls on the peak syllable of each rhythm unit after the primary stressed syllable until the penultimate syllable. [...] In all non-verbs the secondary stress falls on the peak of every rhythm unit after the primary stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees on initial primary stress and adds the compound-stem rule, the rhythm-unit account of secondary/tertiary stress, and the length facts (contrastive only in the initial syllable). Data from Kunini village, 1973-74.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is fully predictable: primary stress on the first syllable of the phonological word; each stem of a compound is its own phonological word with its own initial primary stress. Words are organised into rhythm units (a peak syllable plus one or two coda syllables); polysyllabic words divide into two-syllable rhythm units, with a three-syllable unit before the penult in odd-syllabled verbs and a final one-syllable unit in odd-syllabled non-verbs. Vowel length is contrastive only in the initial (stressed) syllable of a word or stem (p. 101); after the first syllable vowel and consonant length is non-contrastive and follows the rhythm (p. 125). No tone is mentioned anywhere in the paper.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Verbs of more than three syllables: secondary stress on the penultimate syllable, tertiary stress on the peak of each rhythm unit between the primary and the penult. Non-verbs: secondary stress on the peak of every rhythm unit after the primary stress. In three-syllable verb rhythm units the second coda syllable is stronger than the first (p. 125).
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds carry an initial primary stress on each stem (two phonological words, e.g. /pa:mlepamle/ 'lightning'). Syllables containing /a/ or /æ/ preceded by a voiced stop are 'articulated with greater force', giving an almost even rhythm within the rhythm unit (p. 124). Footnote: further study of the rhythm unit planned.
new_statements.identity_note: The SIL materials (Fleischmann & Turpeinen 1977, Fleischmann 1970s/1981, Saari 1992) describe the Kunini dialect (eastern Bine, near Daru; 1977 data from four months in Kunini 1973-74; the OPD header mislabels the language code as [ORM]). Döhler's ELAR deposit and dictionary describe Irukupi/Drageli (western Bine; Döhler's own dialect paragraph has a typo calling both groups 'eastern'). All are bine1240 / ISO bon.
